subject: Behavioral Economics
title: The Just-World Hypothesis
description: A tiny lesson with a big payoff: The Just-World Hypothesis.

hook.text: When told a student won a lottery, observers rated her as more hardworking. Luck felt like merit.

buildup.text: Lerner found people blame victims because admitting randomness threatens the belief in fairness.

discovery.text: Just-world hypothesis: people need to believe the world is fair, so they rationalize all outcomes.

twist.text: This leads to victim blaming. 'They must have done something wrong' preserves our sense of safety.

climax.text: The world isn't fair. Accepting that is uncomfortable but opens the door to empathy and real help.

punchline.text: Fairness is a wish, not a law of nature.

quiz.question: What does the just-world hypothesis cause people to do?
options: Blame victims to preserve their belief in fairness

details.summary: The just world hypothesis is the belief that the world is fundamentally fair: good things happen to good people and bad things happen to bad people. This belief leads to victim blaming and reduces sympathy for those experiencing misfortune.
details.whyItMatters: The just world belief provides psychological comfort but distorts moral judgment. It causes people to blame victims of crime, poverty, and illness, attributing their suffering to personal failings rather than circumstance or systemic factors.
takeaways: People believe the world is fair and outcomes are deserved
This belief leads to blaming victims for their own misfortune
The just world hypothesis reduces support for social safety nets

faq.question: Why do people cling to the belief that the world is fair?
faq.answer: Believing in a just world provides psychological security. If bad things only happen to people who deserve them, then being a good person keeps you safe. Acknowledging random misfortune is threatening because it means it could happen to anyone.

faq.question: How does the just world hypothesis affect attitudes toward poverty?
faq.answer: People who strongly believe in a just world attribute poverty to laziness rather than structural factors. They are less supportive of welfare programs because they perceive recipients as deserving their situation through poor choices.
